catalog_quote: Stress is not a phonemic feature in Bhadarwahi language. Generally a syllable having a consonant cluster gets stressed. As in: kənne ‘and’, dʒəkʰno ‘bite’, həɖɖ ‘bone’ In a di-syllabic vowel where both the syllables having vowel sounds (if vowel is of same length), the first one gets stressed. As in: piɳo ‘to drink’, sukkʰo ‘dry’, kʰɑɳo ‘to eat’. The first syllable gets stressed if it is a low front vowel or a back vowel. As in: dure ‘far’, deli ‘Delhi’. The second syllable gets stressed when the first syllable having a short vowel. As in: həro ‘green’, həsno ‘to laugh’, and dərjɑ ‘river’. In a tri-syllabic word if first and third syllable having long vowel and the middle vowel is short; the initial vowel gets stressed.

sources.citation: Varma, Siddheshwar. 1948. The Bhalesi Dialect. Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal Monograph Series IV. Calcutta. (Bhalesi = Glottolog dialect of bhad1241; Varma a trained phonetician, fieldwork 1928)
sources.quote: 'In the case of a few words of two syllables, the comparative shortening of the second syllable indicates that in some period there was a strong tendency to accent the first syllable of words ... But the accent of many words, especially of compound words, indicates that the present predominant tendency is to accent a syllable other than the first syllable' [list of compounds stressed on 2nd member]. p.14: 'An interesting variation of meaning is indicated by the difference of accent in the past participle and the perfect participle. The words have the same form, but the meaning differs with the
sources.note: Phonetician's first-hand 'Accent' section (pp. 13-14) for the Bhalesi dialect of bhad1241 with stress-marked forms and a participle accent contrast ('biJJo vs bij'jo; Bhad. 'biJJore vs bhu'ore) that qualifies Dwivedi's 'stress is not phonemic'; worth citing as a caution/secondary source in the record.
sources.venue: Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal Monograph Series IV

sources.citation: Varma, Siddheshwar (1936). The Rudhārī dialect (High Rudhārī). Indian Linguistics 6. pp. 128-196.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.note: This work describes High Rudhari (the Rudhari dialect of Rudhar, Chineni jagir, Jammu; grouped by the author with Khasali, with Bhadarwahi as a neighbouring lingua franca that 'exerts considerable influence on Rudhari', p. 440). No statement about Bhadarwahi stress or tone. Bhadarwahi appears only as comparative forms with stress marks ('bholo 'he will be', 'galglo 'he will start', 'ghorero 'of the horse', 'oro 'arrived', 'goro 'gone', 'khoro 'eaten', 'merta 'having died', 'ketta 'having cut', 'tusa 'you (women)', 'asa 'we (women)', 'ghore-sei 'with a horse/stone', 'ghorepur 'on the horse'),…

sources.citation: Varma, Siddheshwar. 1945. Indian dialects in phonetic transcription II: Bhadarwahi, Bhalesi and Khashali. Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal, Letters, XI: 91-94+.
sources.quote: No rule statement; a stress-marked phonetic text of Bhadarwahi (e.g. 'uttrero, 'gallipur, 'larne, 'lagore, u'lhora, di'ha'ro, ki'ore 'they have/had been done') — primary data showing mostly initial stress with non-initial stress on some prefixed/derived forms and perfect participles.
sources.locator: pp. 91-94, North Wind and the Sun text (1) Bhadarwahi, with notes
sources.note: Stress-marked Bhadarwahi text by a phonetician — the only primary stress-annotated data found; useful to test Dwivedi's weight/initial-default statements against tokens.
sources.venue: Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Bengal, Letters, XI: 91-94+

sources.quote: Incidental only: 'The doubling of the t in the past participle is due to accent' (Bhadrawahi kuttu); in the PADARI section, 'Mr. Bailey often writes nouns and participles as ending in short a ... This probably merely indicates that the accent is on the preceding syllable.' (The quick-screen 'contra' quote in our record is this Padari remark, not a Bhadrawahi statement.) No stress rule.
